INDIO, California (CNN) -- For some concertgoers, the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival really kicked into action on Day Two. Festival attendees enjoy the music Saturday, Day Two of the Coachella music festival in Indio, California. Day One was leisurely and pleasant -- the weather was mild, the acts were fairly mellow and the big headliner was Paul McCartney. On Day Two, someone took the dial and turned it up a notch, as the desert sun beat down a little harder, the music pumped a little louder and the crowds who packed the VIP tent threw a little more attitude. There were the usual celebrity sightings. Jake Gyllenhaal and Reese Witherspoon snuck in the back just as rapper M.I.A. hit the stage, Paris Hilton took in Travis Barker and DJ AM's set in the Sahara tent and David Hasselhoff was spotted making out with a mystery lady near the restrooms. Forty-six acts performed on five stages scattered about the grassy field of the Empire Polo Club near Palm Springs, California. Massive eco-friendly art installations fashioned from scrap metal and reclaimed wood doubled as shelter from the heat, as well as mini-stages for dancers and performance artists. There was good buzz for thenewno2, an indie-pop band fronted by Oli Hecks and Dhani Harrison, whose vocals are reminiscent of his late father, George, but warmer, and less haunting. "It's the first festival we've ever played, and our 12th gig overall," said Harrison. "Normally with festivals, people come to check you out, stand in the back, and then move on pretty quickly, even if they like you -- but people stayed! It's the best performance we've ever had." Unfortunately Fleet Foxes was not so lucky. The Seattle,Washington, group's delicate baroque harmonies were drowned out by the world music beats of Thievery Corporation's percussion section bleeding over from the neighboring main stage, as one of their female vocalists crowd-surfed. As usual, the day's line-up was a mix of up-and-coming indie artists sprinkled with tried-and-true veteran acts. The Killers have played Coachella in both capacities. The Las Vegas, Nevada, quartet received their first invitation from festival organizers in 2004, the same year their debut album, "Hot Fuss," was released. "We played at 11:30 a.m. in a tent. It was 150 degrees out, and backstage, it smelled like horse droppings," said drummer Ronnie Vannucci, referencing the fact that there are certain consequences to holding an event on a polo field in the desert. This time, as the marquee act, The Killers enjoyed their own backstage compound decked out with a white picket fence, tablecloths and festive party lights in the shape of daisies. Palm trees gently swayed in the distance, silhouetted against the desert backdrop. You could hear the crowd going crazy for a feisty M.I.A. slotted on the main stage before The Killers. Vannucci and his three bandmates had just rolled in on their tour bus from Vegas. He spoke with CNN while warming up his hands and wrists with drumming exercises. "With festivals, you have to realize the audience is not necessarily there to see YOU. So we'll play some stuff off our new album, 'Day and Age,' and work in some songs that everybody knows, like 'Mr. Brightside' from our first album." Half an hour later, The Killers took the stage, opening their set with their latest hit, "Human." Frontman Brandon Flowers soon had the crowd singing the along to the perplexing lyrics, "Are we human, or are we dancer?" At Coachella, it doesn't matter if you're human or if you're dancer. But if you're dancer, you'll probably be relegated to one of the mini-stages inside an art installation. "The first time I heard about Coachella 10 years ago, I thought, 'That could be the cool festival here in America," said Vannucci. "It's since become a successful festival with good bands, swarms of people coming in from all over the world -- even art elements. It's strange to think we're headlining one night."

INDIO, California (CNN) -- For some concertgoers, the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival truly hit its stride on Day Two.

Festival attendees enjoyed the music on Saturday, the second day of the Coachella music festival in Indio, California. Day One had unfolded at a leisurely, pleasant pace—the weather was mild, the acts relatively subdued, and the marquee headliner was Paul McCartney. On Day Two, however, someone seemed to turn up the dial: the desert sun beat down with greater intensity, the music thundered louder, and the crowds packing the VIP tent carried themselves with a touch more swagger.

The usual celebrity sightings were in abundance. Jake Gyllenhaal and Reese Witherspoon slipped in through the back just as rapper M.I.A. took the stage, Paris Hilton took in Travis Barker and DJ AM's set beneath the Sahara tent, and David Hasselhoff was spotted sharing an embrace with a mystery companion near the restrooms.

Forty-six acts performed across five stages scattered throughout the grassy expanse of the Empire Polo Club near Palm Springs, California. Massive, eco-conscious art installations—crafted from scrap metal and reclaimed wood—offered welcome shelter from the heat while doubling as intimate stages for dancers and performance artists.

There was considerable buzz surrounding thenewno2, an indie-pop outfit fronted by Oli Hecks and Dhani Harrison, whose vocals evoke the spirit of his late father, George, yet carry a warmer, less haunting quality. "It's the first festival we've ever played, and our twelfth gig overall," Harrison remarked. "Normally at festivals, people wander over to check you out, linger in the back, and move on fairly quickly—even if they enjoy what they hear. But this time, people stayed. It was the best performance we've ever given."

Fleet Foxes, unfortunately, fared less well. The Seattle-based group's delicate, baroque harmonies were nearly overwhelmed by the world-music percussion of Thievery Corporation bleeding over from the neighboring main stage, even as one of their female vocalists took to crowd-surfing.

As is customary, the day's lineup blended rising indie talent with seasoned, dependable veterans. The Killers have graced Coachella in both roles. The Las Vegas quartet received their first invitation from festival organizers in 2004, the same year their debut album, "Hot Fuss," was released. "We played at 11:30 in the morning in a tent. It was 150 degrees out, and backstage smelled like horse droppings," recalled drummer Ronnie Vannucci, alluding to the inevitable consequences of hosting an event on a polo field in the desert.

This time, as the night's headlining act, The Killers enjoyed their own backstage compound, complete with a white picket fence, linen-draped tables, and festive daisy-shaped party lights. Palm trees swayed gently in the distance, their silhouettes etched against the desert horizon. The roar of the crowd for a spirited M.I.A., performing on the main stage just before The Killers, could be heard from afar.

Vannucci and his three bandmates had just arrived by tour bus from Las Vegas. He spoke with CNN while loosening his hands and wrists with drumming exercises. "With festivals, you have to remember the audience isn't necessarily there just to see you," he explained. "So we'll play material from our new album, 'Day and Age,' while working in songs everyone knows, like 'Mr. Brightside' from our first record."

Half an hour later, The Killers took the stage, launching their set with their latest hit, "Human." Frontman Brandon Flowers soon had the crowd singing along to the enigmatic refrain, "Are we human, or are we dancer?"

At Coachella, it hardly matters whether you're human or dancer—though if you're the latter, you'll likely find yourself relegated to one of the smaller stages tucked inside an art installation.

"The first time I heard about Coachella, ten years ago, I thought, 'This could become the cool festival here in America,'" Vannucci reflected. "It's since grown into a truly successful festival—great bands, swarms of people arriving from all over the world, even striking art elements woven throughout. It's strange to think we're now headlining a night."

By comparison, Day Two crackled with a different kind of energy—louder, faster, and charged with anticipation.

# The Killers Close Out Coachella With a Career-Spanning Victory Lap

The Empire Polo Club's dust had barely settled on Sunday night when The Killers took the main stage and reminded everyone exactly why they've earned their place among the festival's most reliable headliners. Two decades into their career, Brandon Flowers and company delivered a set that felt less like a nostalgia trip and more like a statement: this band still knows how to command a field of 100,000 people.

The Las Vegas outfit opened with a stripped-down take on "Mr. Brightside" — a bold choice, saving the anthemic build for later — before diving into a setlist that balanced deep cuts from *Hot Fuzz* era B-sides with the stadium-sized hits that have defined them. "Somebody Told Me" and "Spaceman" got the polo grounds moving early, while a mid-set run through "Human" turned into a full-crowd singalong that you could probably hear from Indio proper.

Flowers, resplendent in a sequined jacket that caught every beam of the production's elaborate light show, played the consummate frontman — part preacher, part rock star, all charisma. He brought out a surprise guest for "Shot at the Night," though the crowd's biggest reaction may have come during "All These Things That I've Done," when the gospel choir walked out and the entire field seemed to levitate.

What made the night resonate, though, was the sense of history. The Killers first played Coachella in 2004, a scrappy young band from Vegas riding the buzz of *Hot Fuzz* singles and not much else. Twenty years later, they closed the same festival as certified legends.

"We played the Gobi tent back in '04 — I don't think there were more than a few thousand people even paying attention," drummer Ronnie Vannucci said backstage after the show. "Now we're headlining the main stage, closing the whole thing out. It's wild to think about. Back then we were just hoping people would remember our name. Now people are singing lyrics back at us that they've known their whole lives. That's not something you take for granted, ever."

The set closed, predictably and perfectly, with "When You Were Young," fireworks arcing over the polo fields as Flowers held the final note into the desert night. It was a fitting bookend for a band that has spent two decades chasing that arena-sized euphoria — and on Sunday, they caught it completely.

For a festival often obsessed with what's next, The Killers offered a rare, welcome reminder: sometimes the best moments are the ones that have been earned over time.

# Coachella's Second Day: Sonic Journeys and Desert Dreams

**INDIO, Calif.** — Under the punishing afternoon sun, the second day of Coachella unfolded as a study in contrasts—hushed harmonies giving way to defiant beats, all set against a backdrop of towering, surreal art installations that transformed the polo field into something between a music festival and an open-air gallery.

## Harmonies in the Heat

Fleet Foxes arrived early enough in the day that the temperature hadn't yet reached its punishing peak, and their lush, folk-inflected harmonies felt like a balm against the desert heat. The Seattle band's set was a masterclass in vocal layering, with frontman Robin Pecknold leading his bandmates through cascading melodies that seemed to hang in the dry air long after each song ended. Fans sprawled on blankets, swaying gently, many closing their eyes as if the music itself offered shade.

## A Beatle's Legacy, Reimagined

Later in the afternoon, thenewno2—the project fronted by Dhani Harrison, son of George Harrison—brought a moodier, more experimental edge to one of the smaller stages. Blending psychedelic textures with modern electronic flourishes, the band drew a curious crowd, some clearly there out of reverence for the Harrison name, others discovering the atmospheric, guitar-driven soundscapes for the first time. It was a quieter triumph, but no less compelling for it.

## M.I.A. Ignites the Field

If the day had been building toward something, it arrived with M.I.A. The British provocateur turned her set into a full-throttle celebration of noise, politics, and rhythm. Backed by thunderous bass and her signature clattering percussion, she prowled the stage with unrelenting energy, whipping the crowd into a frenzy that had been simmering since sundown. Tracks blending Tamil rap influences with dancehall and grime had the audience pressed shoulder to shoulder, fists in the air, the desert dust kicking up under thousands of stomping feet. It was chaotic, political, and undeniably electric—M.I.A. doesn't do subtlety, and the crowd wouldn't have wanted her to.

## Art as Escape

Between sets, festivalgoers wandered the polo field's art installations, which have become as integral to the Coachella experience as the music itself. Massive sculptural works loomed over the crowd, offering shade, shadow, and no small amount of Instagram-worthy backdrops. Some installations invited interaction—climbing structures and reflective surfaces that turned attendees into part of the artwork—while others simply stood as strange, beautiful monuments amid the chaos, offering a moment of visual meditation between the sonic assault of back-to-back performances.

By the time the sun dipped below the horizon and the temperature finally began to break, day two had cemented itself as a day of duality: intimate and explosive, contemplative and unrestrained. As always, Coachella found a way to hold all of it—the folk hush, the experimental drift, the political fire, and the strange, sculptural dreams scattered across the polo field—within a single, sprawling desert afternoon.

# Music Festival's Two Faces: McCartney's Gentle Nostalgia Gives Way to High-Voltage Second Night

**GLASTONBURY-ADJACENT FESTIVAL GROUNDS** — What began Friday as an evening of warm nostalgia transformed into a pulse-pounding celebration of raw energy by Saturday night, as festival organizers delivered a study in contrasts that left the estimated 85,000 attendees experiencing two entirely different musical worlds.

Sir Paul McCartney opened the festival's main stage Friday with a career-spanning three-hour set that leaned heavily into the Beatles legend's gentler catalog. Backed by soft lighting and minimal pyrotechnics, the 82-year-old icon moved through acoustic renditions of "Blackbird" and "Here, There and Everywhere," pausing frequently to share stories from his decades-long career.

"It felt like being at your grandfather's fireside," said Maria Chen, 34, who traveled from Portland to attend. "Everyone was just swaying, some people crying. It was beautiful, but it definitely wasn't a mosh pit kind of night."

The mellow atmosphere extended across Friday's supporting lineup, with folk acts and singer-songwriters dominating secondary stages. Concession lines moved slowly as attendees lingered over craft cocktails and artisanal food trucks, many settling into lawn chairs rather than crowding toward barricades.

That leisurely pace evaporated by Saturday afternoon.

The festival's second day shifted dramatically toward heavier, bass-driven programming, with electronic and rock acts drawing significantly younger, more kinetic crowds. By early evening, mosh pits had formed near the main stage, and security reported a noticeable uptick in crowd-surfing incidents compared to Friday's subdued gathering.

"It's night and day — literally," said festival security coordinator James Whitfield. "Friday, our biggest job was helping people find lost lawn chairs. Saturday, we've got a completely different energy to manage."

Headliners including a chart-topping electronic duo and a rock band known for pyrotechnic-heavy performances kept crowds standing and screaming well past midnight, a stark departure from Friday's earlier, quieter conclusion.

Festival organizer Denise Rowland said the programming contrast was intentional. "We wanted to honor different eras and energies of live music," she said. "Paul represents this incredible songcraft and legacy. Saturday is about visceral, in-the-moment intensity. Both are valid ways to experience live music."

Attendees seemed to embrace the whiplash. Many who described Friday as "healing" returned Saturday ready for something entirely different.

"I needed both nights," Chen admitted, having stayed for the festival's second day despite her quieter preferences. "Friday fed my soul. Saturday, I just wanted to scream and jump around. Turns out I needed that too."

The festival continues through Sunday, with organizers promising a "balanced" final day blending elements of both energies.

# Coachella 2009: Sun, Sustainability, and Star Power in the Desert

**INDIO, CALIFORNIA** — The Empire Polo Club transformed once again into a sprawling oasis of music, art, and celebrity spectacle as Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival returned for its tenth anniversary edition. Against the backdrop of the Santa Rosa Mountains, three days of performances drew a diverse crowd eager to witness reunions, breakout sets, and an increasingly ambitious commitment to environmental consciousness.

## Headliners Deliver Reunion Magic

Paul McCartney's Friday night headlining set became one of the weekend's most talked-about moments, with the former Beatle drawing an enormous crowd that stretched back farther than festival organizers had anticipated.

"I've played some big shows in my time, but looking out at this sea of people under the desert sky—it's something else entirely," McCartney reportedly told the audience between songs, referencing the festival's unique setting.

The Killers closed out the festival, with frontman Brandon Flowers noting backstage, "Coming back to Coachella feels like coming home. This is where bands get to show what they're really about, no filters, just the music and the moment."

Perhaps the most anticipated reunion came from The Killers' fellow desert-rock contemporaries Throbbing Gristle, whose reformation brought industrial music pioneers back to a new generation of festivalgoers.

## Celebrity Sightings Dominate the Polo Fields

As always, the crowd itself became part of the show. Paparazzi and gossip blogs buzzed with sightings throughout the weekend:

- **Leonardo DiCaprio** was spotted lounging in the VIP section, reportedly deep in conversation with members of Kings of Leon after their Saturday set.
- **Kate Bosworth and Alex Greenwald** made a notable couple appearance, drawing attention as they wandered the grounds hand-in-hand.
- **Gerard Butler** was photographed dancing enthusiastically during Franz Ferdinand's set, prompting nearby fans to snap photos rather than watch the stage.
- Rumors swirled about a possible on-site reconciliation between two musicians from a prominent indie band, though neither party addressed the speculation directly.

The festival's famous "fashion show" atmosphere continued unabated, with flower crowns, vintage band tees, and daringly minimal desert attire serving as the weekend's unofficial dress code among the celebrity set and civilians alike.

## Art Installations Go Green

Beyond the music, this year's festival placed unprecedented emphasis on sustainability through its acclaimed art program. The Do LaB, long a fixture of Coachella's artistic landscape, unveiled several installations built entirely from reclaimed and recycled materials.

Towering sculptures constructed from repurposed shipping containers and salvaged wood dotted the grounds, while a series of solar-powered light installations illuminated pathways after dark—reducing the festival's reliance on generator power.

One standout piece, an interactive sculpture garden created from recycled plastic bottles collected from previous festival years, invited attendees to add their own contributions throughout the weekend, growing organically as the event progressed.

"We wanted to prove that a festival this size doesn't have to leave a massive footprint," explained one installation artist involved with the Do LaB collective. "Every piece here tells a story about waste and transformation. We're trying to shift how people think about consumption, even in a space designed for celebration."

The festival also expanded its recycling and composting initiatives, with color-coded bins strategically placed throughout the polo grounds and a noticeably increased presence of water refill stations aimed at cutting down on plastic bottle waste.

## A Festival Evolving

As dust settled over the Empire Polo Club on Sunday night, Coachella 2009 seemed to signal a festival maturing into its second decade—one increasingly aware of both its cultural influence and its environmental responsibility, without sacrificing the star-studded spectacle that made it famous in the first place.
